NOVELTY STATEMENT
Standard practice delivers a DESIGN CHANGE via material hardening or geometry profile modification to increase contact hardness or reduce peak Hertzian stress at the gauge corner. My same-class departure is a CONFIGURATION mechanism: implementing a **Dynamic Contact Geometry Shifting** system that actively alters the effective wheel-rail contact patch position away from the gauge corner during curve negotiation. The failure-physics connection is that shifting the contact point laterally out of the high-stress zone of the gauge corner reduces the peak subsurface shear stress that drives Rolling Contact Fatigue (RCF) shelling.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing relation is Hertzian contact stress distribution. For a wheel flange or tread contacting a rail, the peak subsurface shear stress $\tau_{max}$ occurs at a depth $z \approx 0.78a$ and laterally at distance $b \approx 0.5\text{-}0.7a$ from the contact center, where $a$ is the semi-major axis of the contact ellipse.
Magnitude verification: Standard RCF initiation occurs when cyclic $\tau_{max}$ exceeds the fatigue limit of the rail steel (~900-1000 MPa shear). By shifting the contact centroid laterally by $\Delta x = 1.5a$ from the gauge corner (where $a$ is typically 10-15 mm for heavy rail), the local Hertzian stress at the gauge corner location drops by more than 50% because the peak stress moves with the centroid. This reduces the fatigue damage accumulation rate per pass, extending the time to shelling initiation.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
*   **Primary Stated Indicator (Constraint Bind):** Wheel load and lateral force data from existing axle box sensors (ALREADY-RECORDED in most modern locomotive fleets) are the primary indicators. The system monitors the magnitude of the lateral force $F_y$ which directly correlates to the slip and contact stress distribution.
*   **Configuration Hardware:** A lateral wheelset steering actuator (linear actuator, class similar to those used in active suspension) installed on the bogie axle. This is a MATERIAL/GEOMETRY configuration change.
*   **Input Streams:**
    *   Lateral wheel force $F_y$ (ALREADY-RECORDED in standard condition monitoring logs).
    *   Wheel tread profile (from standard periodic wheel laser scanning, ALREADY-RECORDED).
    *   Curve radius (ALREADY-RECORDED in track geometry database).
*   **Reference/Threshold:** The control threshold for actuation is derived from the ratio $F_y / F_z$ (Lateral-to-Vertical load ratio). A DERIVED threshold of $F_y / F_z > 0.3$ indicates high-slip, high-stress conditions at the gauge corner where steering should be active to shift the contact point. This value is derived from standard wheel-rail interaction physics for heavy freight locomotives.
*   **Procedure:** The actuator shifts the wheelset laterally by 2-4 mm relative to the axle housing. This changes the effective contact point on the rail head from the gauge corner to the tread/foot interface, where the rail steel is thicker and has a higher fatigue limit.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
*   **Installability:** Same as active suspension or existing bogie maintenance. No new sensor types required; uses existing wheel force sensors and wheel scan data.
*   **Operability:** Passive when $F_y/F_z < 0.3$. Active steering requires minor hydraulic/pneumatic power, class-comparable to existing brake systems.
*   **Maintenance:** The actuator is a standard linear motion component, similar class to door actuators or suspension dampers. No exotic material replacement.
*   **Cost Class:** Higher than passive profile grinding (standard practice), but comparable to active bogie systems already in some locomotive classes. The burden is in the mechanical actuator, not in new instrumentation.

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol:
1.  Select a test curve with known radius and gauge corner RCF history.
2.  Run the locomotive with the lateral steering actuator enabled.
3.  Record $F_y/F_z$ ratios and wheelset lateral displacement from existing sensors.
4.  Measure rail head temperature and use non-contact laser profilometry (if available on the rail, or via post-test inspection) to verify contact point shift.
Pass/Fail Thresholds:
*   PASS: The contact point shifts laterally off the gauge corner by >1.5 mm when $F_y/F_z > 0.3$.
*   PASS: Post-test inspection shows reduced surface roughness or delayed shelling initiation compared to a control run without steering.
*   FAIL: No lateral shift observed, or increased wear on the new contact point exceeds the reduction in gauge corner shelling rate (net damage increase).
Duration: One full curve transit sequence.
Kill Criterion: If the shifted contact point creates a new stress concentration that causes spalling or excessive wear within 1000 passes.

CONSTRAINT BIND (PREDICTOR)
The monitored indicator is the **Lateral Wheel Force ($F_y$)**. This is the PRIMARY stated indicator because $F_y$ directly determines the contact stress distribution and slip at the gauge corner. The wheelset lateral displacement is a secondary indicator that validates the mechanism's actuation but does not define the failure threshold. The system only operates when the primary indicator $F_y/F_z$ exceeds the derived physics threshold, ensuring the intervention is targeted to high-stress conditions.
